name: Presentation to Management
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Ten Minutes, One Ask: Presenting to People Who Don't Want to Hear About Blockchain
lesson.summary: This chapter covers compressing a full architecture report into a short executive presentation that states the ask plainly, names the rejected alternatives, and anticipates the biases and pushback that come from a management audience.
lesson.body:
The architecture report is thorough on purpose, and that is precisely why it cannot be the thing you hand an executive team and expect them to read before a decision meeting. Management's job is to decide, not to audit your utility tree, and a presentation that tries to walk them through the full document in the room either runs out of time before reaching the recommendation or buries the recommendation so deep that the meeting ends with let's take this offline, which is where good recommendations go to die.

The discipline here is compression without distortion: cut volume aggressively while keeping the reasoning honest, which is harder than either cutting volume carelessly or keeping every caveat. A useful structure is five slides, in this order: the problem, framed in terms management already cares about, not in blockchain vocabulary; the options considered, named plainly, with the rejected ones getting one line each rather than being omitted, because an executive who later hears about the rejected option from someone else and realizes it was never mentioned will trust the next recommendation less; the recommendation itself, stated as a decision to be made, not a technology to admire; cost and timeline, in the roadmap's actual stages so the ask is bounded, this pilot, this budget, this review date, not an open-ended commitment; and risks, the two or three that actually matter, each paired with its mitigation from the architecture report's risk register.

Anticipate the questions that come from management's own biases, because they have them too, just different ones from the biases that push engineers toward adopting new technology. The most common is a version of bandwagon pressure: our competitor announced a blockchain pilot last quarter, why aren't we further along. The grounded answer doesn't dismiss the concern, it reframes it through the decision flowchart: we ran the same evaluation any credible blockchain adoption should run, and it told us where blockchain fits our situation and where it doesn't, which is a stronger position than matching a competitor's announcement without knowing whether their situation actually matches ours. Another common one is authority bias dressed as due diligence, the vendor's sales engineer said their platform handles this natively, which the presenter should be ready to answer by pointing at the pilot's actual measured results rather than arguing with the vendor's claim directly, since evidence from your own pilot outranks a vendor's claim about their own product every time, and saying so plainly is not disrespectful, it's the entire point of having run a pilot.

Walk through how this plays out for Meridian. The problem slide doesn't open with blockchain, it opens with a cold-chain break in the last two years took three weeks to trace to its source during a recall, and regulators are now asking for auditable proof, not paperwork, before the next inspection cycle. The options slide names three: continue improved manual auditing, a shared database run by a neutral third party, and a permissioned ledger among the four parties, with one line each on why the first two were rejected. The recommendation slide states the pilot, its scope, and its two fixed success metrics, matching the recommendation memo word for word rather than introducing new phrasing that could be read as a different ask. The cost and timeline slide shows the four-stage roadmap with the pilot's capped budget and its review date. The risk slide surfaces the rural connectivity gap honestly, with the store-and-forward fix already noted as addressed, which preempts the most likely tough question in the room rather than waiting to be caught by it.

When an executive asks, as one almost always does, why not just use a regular database, the presenter's answer traces straight back to gate three of the decision flowchart: because no single party here is trusted by the other three to hold the master copy honestly, the carrier has an incentive to round temperature logs favorably, and that's exactly the situation blockchain is suited for and a shared database isn't. That answer works because it isn't improvised, it's the same reasoning that has been carried, unchanged, from the decision flowchart through the architecture report to this slide. A presentation that can answer any question by pointing at a specific, already-documented step in that chain is what actually earns the room's trust, far more than polish or confidence in the delivery.
